slides.title: A neural network is a weighted, adaptive signal-processing system
points: Core definition

A neural network is built from simple processing units connected by weighted links. Each unit receives inputs, combines them, applies an activation function, and passes a signal forward or around a network.
Why it matters
The network does not need a hand-written rule for every case. It adjusts weights from examples so that its input-output mapping improves for a task.
slides.takeaway: The network does not need a hand-written rule for every case. It adjusts weights from examples so that its input-output mapping improves for a task.

Synapses

extraPoints: Many simple units together can express complex behavior.
slides.takeaway: Information-processing cells inspire artificial processing units.

slides.takeaway: Activation function controls the neuron's output response.

slides.title: The neuron model is compact enough to write as one equation
points: y = φ( Σ wi xi + b )
xi are input signals; wi are synaptic weights.
b is the bias, equivalent to a weight connected to a constant input.
φ is the activation function that introduces a controlled nonlinearity.
slides.takeaway: xi are input signals; wi are synaptic weights.
slides.formula: y = φ( Σ wi xi + b )

slides.title: Single-layer feedforward networks are the simplest classifiers
points: Structure
The input layer distributes signals to output neurons. There is no hidden computation layer; the trainable weights sit on the links into the output layer.
Consequence
The decision boundary is linear in the input space. This is enough for separable problems, but not for problems requiring nonlinear boundaries.
slides.takeaway: The input layer distributes signals to output neurons. There is no hidden computation layer; the trainable weights sit on the links into the output layer.

slides.title: Rosenblatt's perceptron is a trainable binary classifier
points: Historical role
Introduced as an early learning machine for pattern classification.
Inputs
Feature vector x represents the pattern to be classified.
Weights
Weights are adjusted from labeled examples.
extraPoints: A hard threshold chooses one of two classes.
slides.takeaway: Introduced as an early learning machine for pattern classification.

slides.title: The perceptron computes a weighted sum and applies a threshold
points: y = sign(wᵀx + b)
w is the weight vector and b is the bias.
The sign of the induced local field assigns the input to one of two classes.
The separating surface is wᵀx + b = 0.
slides.takeaway: w is the weight vector and b is the bias.

slides.title: Geometrically, a perceptron draws a hyperplane
points: wᵀx + b = 0
Points on one side map to class +1.
Points on the other side map to class -1.
In two dimensions the hyperplane is a line; in higher dimensions it is a plane-like separator.
slides.takeaway: Points on the other side map to class -1.

slides.title: Perceptron learning changes weights only when a pattern is misclassified
points: w(new) = w(old) + η d x
η is the learning-rate parameter.
d is the desired class label, commonly +1 or -1.
The correction moves the separating hyperplane toward classifying x correctly.
slides.takeaway: d is the desired class label, commonly +1 or -1.

slides.title: The convergence theorem needs linear separability
points: Condition
A training set is linearly separable if at least one hyperplane can classify every training example correctly.
Guarantee
For linearly separable data and a suitable fixed learning rate, the perceptron learning rule reaches a solution in a finite number of updates.
slides.takeaway: A training set is linearly separable if at least one hyperplane can classify every training example correctly.

slides.title: Convergence is a statement about finding a separator, not about finding the best separator
points: The theorem says the algorithm will stop if a separating hyperplane exists.
It does not say the separator is unique.
It does not maximize margin; different starting weights can reach different valid solutions.
If the data are not linearly separable, the basic perceptron can keep updating indefinitely.
slides.takeaway: The theorem says the algorithm will stop if a separating hyperplane exists.
slides.formula: The theorem says the algorithm will stop if a separating hyperplane exists.

slides.title: Nonseparable patterns reveal the perceptron's limitation
points: What fails
If two classes overlap or require a nonlinear boundary, no single hyperplane can classify all examples correctly.
Why it matters
This limitation motivates multilayer networks and nonlinear representation learning in later modules.
slides.takeaway: If two classes overlap or require a nonlinear boundary, no single hyperplane can classify all examples correctly.

slides.title: Bayes classification provides the statistical gold standard
points: Bayes classification assigns an input to the class with the largest posterior probability.
It minimizes probability of classification error when the true class distributions are known.
For Gaussian class-conditional densities, the decision boundary depends on means, covariance, and prior probabilities.
slides.takeaway: Bayes classification assigns an input to the class with the largest posterior probability.

slides.title: A Gaussian environment can make the Bayes boundary linear
points: Equal covariance case
When two Gaussian classes share the same covariance matrix, the Bayes decision boundary is linear in x.
Perceptron connection
A perceptron also implements a linear boundary. Under this condition, its boundary form matches the Bayes classifier form.
slides.takeaway: When two Gaussian classes share the same covariance matrix, the Bayes decision boundary is linear in x.

slides.title: Example: AND is linearly separable, XOR is not
points: AND can be separated by one straight boundary.
XOR cannot be separated by one straight boundary.
This is why Module 2 moves into multilayer perceptrons.
slides.takeaway: AND can be separated by one straight boundary.
